extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students in mathematics; readers with preliminary training in geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of axiomatic/projective geometry: introducing ideal elements, projection, homogeneous coordinates, duality, cross-ratio, conics, and straightedge constructions; aimed at readers with some prior mathematical training. Focus is on definitions, principles, and proofs that form the foundation of projective geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve incidence axiom (through any two points one line)
rubrics_metrics.description: "through any two points one and only one straight line may be drawn" (axiom of geometry) — a law to be preserved when extending the domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that when enlarging the domain (adding ideal elements) we must preserve the laws which governed the original domain; in particular the uniqueness of the line through two points motivates the choice of one ideal point per line and a single line at infinity. This axiom is used as a guiding constraint when defining ideal elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add exactly one ideal point per line (point at infinity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agree to add to the ordinary points on each line a single "ideal" point (the point at infinity on the line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ideal point belongs to all lines parallel to the given line and to no other lines. Only one ideal point per line is added in order to preserve the law that through any two points one and only one line may be drawn (if a line contained two points at infinity common to every parallel line, many lines would pass through those two 'points').

rubrics_metrics.name: Add a single line at infinity containing all ideal points
rubrics_metrics.description: Add to the ordinary lines in a plane a single "ideal" line (the line at infinity) containing all the ideal points in the plane and no other points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This convention is forced if we wish to preserve the law that every two points determine a line and that every two lines intersect in a point. The line at infinity is uniquely determined by these requirements; any two ideal points determine this unique line, which contains no ordinary points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret points at infinity as families of parallel lines
rubrics_metrics.description: A point at infinity is determined or is represented by any family of parallel lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text compares this to irrational numbers determined by sequences; the notation (e.g., symbol 'oo') is a convenient way of indicating parallelism and removes exceptional-case enumeration. This interpretation is intended to make expressions that covered ordinary cases also cover parallel cases automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve incidence relations under extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions regarding points and lines at infinity are chosen so that laws governing the incidence relation between ordinary points and lines continue to hold in the extended domain of points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After adding ideal elements, finding the intersection of two lines is always possible; statements about collinear points, concurrent lines, etc., that involve only points, lines, and incidence are invariant under projection in the extended sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection yields biunique correspondence when extended elements included
rubrics_metrics.description: A projection of one plane onto another from a center establishes a correspondence between points and lines of the two planes which is biunique without exception once ideal elements are introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptional cases (projecting rays parallel to the target plane) correspond to points/lines at infinity; after the agreement that such exceptions map to ideal elements, the correspondence between points and lines is one-to-one and onto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operate with elements at infinity via ordinary points in a projected plane
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements at infinity in a plane may be operated with simply by operating with the corresponding ordinary points in a plane coordinated with it by a projection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a concrete method: realize points at infinity of a plane by lines through a center in space corresponding to ordinary points of another plane; hence computations and proofs may be reduced to ordinary points in a projected model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend to three dimensions: line and plane at infinity
rubrics_metrics.description: In three dimensions, each plane has a line at infinity; introduce a plane at infinity consisting of all points at infinity of the space and containing all lines at infinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each ordinary plane intersects the plane at infinity in its line at infinity. The same ideas generalize to higher dimensions though less intuitively visualizable by projection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define cross-ratio involving points at infinity by limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If A, B, C are three ordinary points on l, then (A B C oo) is defined as the limit of (A B C P) as P recedes to infinity along l; in practice (A B C oo) = CA/CB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: as P → ∞ along l, PA/PB → 1, so (ABCoo) = CA/CB. Consequence: if (ABCoo) = −1 then C is the midpoint of AB; midpoint and point at infinity divide the segment harmonically. Exercises ask for analogous cross-ratio values for parallel lines or when one line is the line at infinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use elements at infinity to eliminate exceptional-case statements
rubrics_metrics.description: With elements at infinity it is no longer necessary to state explicitly the exceptional cases that arise when lines are parallel; they become ordinary cases in the extended language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central vs parallel projection distinction disappears (parallel projection = projection from a point at infinity). The general principle: by moving to the extended domain one can write uniform statements and proofs without separate exceptions for parallels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective class and invariance principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The projective class of a figure F is the class of all figures into which F may be carried by projective transformations; projective properties are invariant under projection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove any projective theorem for F, it suffices to prove it for any member of its projective class (one can often choose a member for which the theorem is simpler to prove, e.g. by projecting some points to infinity). This strategy is illustrated in proofs of Desargues, Pascal, Brianchon, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric methods may be used but projective definitions can be intrinsic
rubrics_metrics.description: Some proofs (e.g., the given proof of Desargues's theorem) may use metric notions such as segment length, but projective transformations can be defined intrinsically (e.g., as maps preserving cross-ratio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that while a proof may use metric arguments, an intrinsic ('in the plane') projective proof exists if projective transformations are defined via cross-ratio preservation; analytic methods can also supply intrinsic proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of duality (point-line dual correspondence)
rubrics_metrics.description: In plane projective geometry, point and line are dual elements; drawing a line through a point and marking a point on a line are dual operations. The dual of any true theorem is likewise true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal's and Brianchon's theorems are dual to each other; Desargues's theorem and its converse are dual. Duality arises from symmetry in homogeneous coordinates and is often exhibited by presenting dual theorems/proofs side-by-side. Note that duality is a special feature of projective geometry, not of metric notions like angles or lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic viewpoint: coordinates characterize geometric objects
rubrics_metrics.description: In analytic geometry the 'coordinates' of a geometrical object are any set of numbers which characterize that object uniquely (e.g., point by x,y or p,θ; line by ax+by+c=0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern viewpoint starts with pairs (x,y) and calls them points; algebraic/analytic methods provide a rigorous and often simpler treatment of projective notions, including points at infinity via homogeneous coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneous coordinates: triples up to scalar
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce homogeneous coordinates: a point is an ordered triple (x,y,z), not all zero; two triples define the same point if they are scalar multiples (tX,tY,tZ) with t ≠ 0. Ordinary points have z ≠ 0; points at infinity have z = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homogeneous coordinates include ideal points and make the point/line description symmetric—points and lines both specified by triples. The coordinates are unique only up to an arbitrary nonzero factor; this is the advantage allowing inclusion of points at infinity in analytic treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation of a line in homogeneous coordinates; line at infinity
rubrics_metrics.description: A straight line in homogeneous coordinates is given by ax + by + cz = 0; the line at infinity is given by z = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The triple (a,b,c) are homogeneous coordinates of the line (also up to scalar). The incidence condition ax+by+cz=0 is symmetric under interchange of the role of point and line coordinates, underpinning duality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry between point and line via homogeneous coordinates
rubrics_metrics.description: There is perfect symmetry: each point and each line is specified by three homogeneous coordinates; the condition that point (x,y,z) lie on line (a,b,c) is ax+by+cz=0, which is symmetric so the point (a,b,c) lies on line (x,y,z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This algebraic symmetry is the basis for duality in projective geometry; it does not hold in ordinary two-coordinate plane until points/lines at infinity are included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective transformations are linear maps on homogeneous coordinates
rubrics_metrics.description: A projective transformation is given analytically by a set of linear equations connecting homogeneous coordinates: x' = a11 x + a12 y + a13 z, y' = a21 x + a22 y + a23 z, z' = a31 x + a32 y + a33 z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defines projective transformations as 3×3 non-singular linear maps on homogeneous triples; projective theorems become statements about behavior of triples under such linear transformations (e.g., cross-ratio preservation follows from algebra).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conics as projections of a circle; projective definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A conic is the projection of a circle on a plane; equivalently, curves defined by second-degree equations arise as such projections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This projective definition places conics naturally in projective geometry. The metric focal definitions (ellipse/hyperbola/parabola via distances to foci/line) are recovered (e.g., via Dandelin spheres) and the analytic representation is quadratic equations ax^2 + by^2 + cxy + dx + ey + f = 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dandelin sphere proof connecting metric focus definition and projection
rubrics_metrics.description: Using two spheres tangent to the cone and touching it along parallel circles yields PFi + PFt = constant for all P on intersection curve, giving focal definition of ellipse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a geometric construction tying the projection-of-circle viewpoint to the metric focal characterization of conics; an exercise suggests analogous argument for hyperbola.

rubrics_metrics.name: Straightedge-only construction program (Steiner) and harmonic sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a fixed circle with center, the compass can be dispensed with; problems 1–18 (Steiner) develop constructions with straightedge alone. A set of four lines through a point is harmonic if cross-ratio (a b c d) = −1; conjugacy defined relative to c & d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook lists concrete straightedge construction problems (construct fourth harmonic line/point, double angle given right/common side, draw parallels, multiply/divide segments given parallelogram or fixed circle, etc.) and recommends solving in order. These constructions illustrate practical use of projective tools and harmonic division.
